The families and friends Of the
service people killed and missing in the
Atlantic airliner accident must wonder
why those people were being carried
in chartered plane and whether they
might have been safer in a military
transport.


The answers are complex, but, in
brief, the soldiers and their families
were on a private airIiner because the
Pentagon in 1860 struck bargain with
the White House and Congress which
put military airplanes largely out of
the passenger business. The Military
Air Transport Service wanted modern
planes and a larger combat-support
assignment. The President and Con-
gress wanted a better civilian aircraft
reserve fleet and an expanded airline
SubSidy-particularly to help those lines
which must compete in overseas traffic
with airlines owned by foreign govern
ments.


A bargain seemed logical at the
time. Following congressional investi-
cation, Congress and the administration
agreed that MATS would give most Of
its passenger business to civilian air.
lines; and Congress voted funds to
modernize MATS and add combat
cargo aircraft. The private airlines
bought better planes, many of which
were pledged to wartime duty for the
services. Apparently everyone bene-
fitted Anyhow, that is why those
soldiers were on a private airliner with
orders in their pockets to report to posts
in Europe.


Would they have been safer on
MATS? The Flying Tiger Line, certifi-
Gated by the CAB, has had two major
accidents this year involving military
people. One, in March, killed lot per-
sons in the western Pacific. Today more
than 20 persons are dead or missing in
the Atlantic. Still, one cannot say that
this airline is less safe than any other.
Like other planes chartered by the
Pentagon, Flying Tiger charter planes
are Safety-checked by MATS and also
meet Federal Aviation Agency stand
ards. Flying Tiger contracts for military
service contain the same conditions ap-
plicable to all military contract flying.


We are told by the Air Force, how
ever, that MATS in its passenger
carrying heyday, was not only the big
gest airline the world had ever seen,
but it had the best safety record. We
are told also that many MATS officers
would feel more comfortable If they
could control directly all of the planes,
and their mechanics, that carry military
passengers.


The Pentagon ordered safety in
Spection frightened late last year after
a crash by chartered plane cost the
lives of "a Army recruits near Rich
mond, Va. 1t is surely time to examine
safety standards again.

MONOCLISSIA, Greece (AP).-The men of this re-

Their women went back to the kitchen after day of
masculine leisure and cafe life.


Once year there comes to life the plot that play
wright Arlsophanes penned 200 years ago. Just in
his comedy Eccesiazousai the women were the masters
OF Monocssia from sunrise to well beyond yes
terday.


The wives circulated. They sat in the cafes. They
drank coffee. The smoked. They played cards and
backgammon. They spouted their opinions on home,
family and community life


The men stayed home cooking wasl 6 houseclean-
ing, sewing and mindng the children. Any husband
caught out on the streets soaked with and
stripped of his clothes.


The males went to bed early The ladies ended their
big day with at the tavern lots of loud music and
rounds of old wine.


The of MonoclisSia are used to their annual day
of servitude. It's been going on since 1922.

LONDON, Jan. 90 (AP).--
Wildcat subway and railroad
strikes for higher pay made
thousands of Londoners late for
work today and threw the cap
ital into one vast traffic jam.


Nearly two million trainless
commuters took to the roads.
Autos, trucks, buses and taxis
were bumper to bumper on the
Thames bridges. Thousands Of
autos converged on London
from the suburbs. Traffic slowed
and then all but halted.


In the southern suburbs
traffic moved at about three
miles an hour.


The chaos resulted from a
one-day strike by the capitals
subway crews and a go-slow by
crewmen on suburban train
services. It would have been
even worse but the city's $4,000
bus drivers refused to join in a
sympathy strike.


Only one in seven of the
capitals subway trains was
running. The subways normally
carry more than 100000 pas
sengers a day.


About half the normal service
IVES running on the southern
region surface railway, which
each day brings in about 100000
commuters from Kent, Surrey
and Sussex.


The strikers say they would
continue to throw London
transport into chaos every
Monday until the government
relaxes its wage freeze policy.
The government has promised a
slight thaw' in April, and
union leaders are not support
ing the strikers.

In announcing that 1000 United
States Marines are being Withdrawn
from Thailand, the Defense Department
explained that President Kennedy has
ordered the action because of general
lessening of tension" along the Laotian
border The move may also be tied in
with the fact that the 14-nation Geneva
Conference on Laos has resumed negoti-
atoms to work out definitive East
West agreement to guarantee the peace
of that country and the independence
and neutrality of its fledgling coalition
regime.


It is noteworthy, however, that the
withdrawal is being carried out on
cautious, gradual basis After its COM
pletion, there will still remain in Thai
land about 1000 of the 5000 American
fighting membranes, Army and Air
Force-Sent there in midMay at the
urgent request of the Royal Thai govern
ment. That request was made because
the Communists had flagrantly violated
the cease-fire in Laos, and there were
fears at the time that their guerrilla
forces might cross the border and attack
the That's But now, some six weeks
later, the rival pro-Western, pro-
Communist and neutralist Laotian fac
lions are collaborating in accord with
the settlement establishing their coali
ton, and there is no present evidence
of a threat to Thailand's peace and
territorial integrity.


Thus the partial pull-out of Marines
makes sense, and presumably all Ameri-
can forces will leave when, as and if
firm guarantees are put into force
against the danger that the Communists
will stage sudden coup in Laos and
strike from there against the That's. 1t
may be assumed, in any event, that the
bulk of our troops in Thailand will stay
there until there is reasonable ground
for confidence that their withdrawal
will not tempt the Reds to attack.
headline: Limited Withdrawal

The Secret Army today
staged its biggest plastic bomb
attack to date in the Moslem
quarter of Oran, touching off
angry Moslem demonstrations.


About 40 bombs exploded,
starting several fires which
firemen brought under control
There was no immediate word
of casualties, although there
were unconfirmed reports that
some Moslems had been trapped
in bomb-wrecked homes.


Heavy attachments of riot

strators could still be heard
The riot forces were able, how

from streaming into European
quarters Of the city.


Women Set Up Cries
Moslems fled into the streets

them panic-stricken. Some
were half dressed and ran
shouting through the streets
Women sent up their tradi-
tional you! You'll" cries.


Demonstrations broke out
here and there, and the demon
strators stoned cars driven by
Europeans on the outskirts of
the quarter.


Police reparted that young
Europeans in another part of
the city were stoning Moslem
cars.


Oran. Algeria's second larg-
est city, is hotbed of Secret
Army activity. Its 400, 900 pop
ulation is about half European,
and the Europeans are over
whelmingly behind the under
ground and its campaign to
keep Algeria French.


Telephone communications
between Algiers and France
were cut today by a strike
of Europeans which also cut
electric power and other serv-
ices. The break lasted several
hours.

The strike by the city's anti
De Gaulle Europeans began
yesterday to protest the arrest
of two members of the Secret
Army earlier this week, and
electric workers in Algiers and
Oran struck today for the
funeral of two fellow workers
killed by Moslem terrorists.


Normal commercial activity
was paralyzed in the Algerian
capital. Most business places
were closed. However, buses
operated normally and govern
ment offices were functioning,

Chairman Murray of the House Civil
Service Committee is, right in holding
that legislation raising postal rates
should have priority over pay increases
for postal and other Federal employees.
For that reason, he is deferring hearings
on various pay proposals pending before
his committee. The postage legislation
already has passed the House, but is
making slow progress on the Senate side.


Politically minded members of both
chambers are always sympathetic to pay
raises for Federal workers, especially
those in the well = organized postal
unions, but they have been reluctant in
the past to boost postal rates. Yet, unless
the rates are increased enough to offset
postal pay hikes, the staggering Post
Office Department deficit will grow even
larger. The orderly and sensible proce-
dure, therefore, is to assure approval of
more postal revenues before voting to
give more pay to Government employees.
We hope the Senate will adopt this
procedure.

rs per cent Of the worlds pop

Thousands of commuters
were stalled on their way to
work today when the South
Capitol Street Bridge stuck
after being swung open for a
tugboat about $50 am.


1t was three hours before
traffic returned to normal.


The four-lane bridge over the
Anacostia River is one of the
main approaches to downtown
Washington from the SOUTH
east. Traffic tunnels onto the
bridge from the Suitland park
way, Indian Head highway and
the new Wilson Bridge over the
Potomac from Virginia.


Traffic backed up quickly
before police could reach the
scene and begin diverting mo-
florists toward the Anacostia
eleventh street, and Sousa
pennsylvania avenue) Bridges.

Even after the bridge was
finally locked into position
again and opened to traffic at
1880, the jam-up of cars re-;
manned huge, extending up to
three miles as the commuter
rush reached its peak.


A few cars had stalled dur

bridge was out, adding to the
confusion, police said.


One car, abandoned by it's
owner on the South Capitol
bridge approach, had to be
moved out of the way by q
highway department crane
after police opened a path for
the crane.


Motorists who could turn
around and head away from
the disabled bridge found
themselves in little better shape
as traffic inched along bumper
to-bumper heading for the two
bridges farther up the Anacos-
tia. Several drivers pulled off
the road and walked into the
city.

waiting in the chill for buses
outside the Justice Department
at Tenth street and Pennsyl-
vania avenue to take them tc
Southeast Washington were tolc
that no buses were available
because they were all stuck il
the traffic beyond the Eleventh
street bridge.


Scores of police rushed to
key intersections to divert traf-
fic away from the worst jams,
directed by the WMAL-police
helicopter. Maryland State
troopers helped in the diversion
farther out the Suitland Park
way.


Bridge operator Archie
Rodgers swung the bridge open
at $50 for a Navy diving school
tug, and discovered to his con-
sternation that when the
bridge swung into the closed
position, some toggle pins re-
fused to go into place, leaving
the bridge about a foot lower
than the approach ramp.


Supervisor Cecil H. Rennoe
= an expert with bridge
mechanisms - eventually got
the toggle pins to work and
the bridge leveled off. But
for many irate commuters, it
was just a little late.

ALEXANDRIA, La, Jan. 6

facilities-but let them stand
10 days.


The decision yesterday was
based on the courts finding
that the State laws interfere
with interstate commerce and
deny equal protection of the
law guaranteed by the 14th
Amendment.


The court asked the Justice
Department and the Interstate
Commerce Commission to file
suggestions for a decree-which
the court said it would file Ill
10 days.


The Justice Department filed
three consolidated suits taking
in Lincoln, Ouachita and
Rapides parishes. State judges
in each of the parishes granted
injunctions that kept terminals
segregated. despite and ICC
order prohibiting segregated
terminal facilities.


Attorney General Jack
Gremillion indicated the State
would appeal the ruling. The
appeal would go directly to the
United States Supreme Court.


Presiding Judge John r.
Brown of the Fifth United
States Circuit Court of Appeals,
Houston, Tex, said Louisiana
segregation laws in transporta-
ton terminals would remain
status quo until the decree is
issued"


Earlier in the hearing the
court dismissed Mr.. Gremil-
lions motion to make the Lou
islana Public Service Commits
sion a party to the Government
suit. He contended the commits
sion was the sole agency reg
ulating intrastate commerce.


Mr.. Gremillion said if the
court ordered segregation signs
removed from the terminals,
the companies involved would
be caught in the middle be-
cause the commission has an
order requiring maintenance of
segregated facilities. The COM
mission order, he said, was not
connected with any law in
volved in the hearing.

them.


Yesterday help came.


Last night, in a bed at st.
Bernardine Hospital, 6-year-old
Julie Clark told her story.


"The plane went down real
fast" she began. "Mommy and
Daddy didn't have a chance to
say anything"


At jules side was her grand
mother. Mrs. Scott King. Mrs.
King stroked jules blond head,
carefully avoiding the big black
bruise near one eye. It was her
son-in-law and daughter, Mr..
and Mrs. William Clark, who
died on the mountainside. Julia
escaped with only bumps,
bruises and exposure.

BERLIN, Feb. 8 (AP).-West
Berlin police reported a big
Communist troop movement in
East Germany today on the
western outskirts of the city.


The police said they saw 80
to 100 army vehicles in a con-
voy moving from the neighbour
hood Of the clientele Bridge,
on the western tip of the Amer
lean sector, along the main road
to Potsdam. The convoy includ-
ed 40 armored personnel car
riers carrying infantry and 40
vehicles towing guns, Western
police said.


The police could not tell
whether the troops were Rus
sian or East German.


At another part of the border.
guards from West Berlin and
East Germany faced each other
almost toe-to-toe with loaded
weapons last night but finally
executed a mutual withdrawal
without bloodshed.


A spokesman for the West
Berlin police gave this account:


An East German border guard
at Chausseestrasse, in the
French sector Of Berlin, shouted
'Nazi swine" at the guard on
the West side.


The East German guard then
aimed a kick at the West Berlin
guard, who punched him in the
chest and sent him Sprawling
on his back. Eastern guards
rushed up with submachine-
guns and the West Berlin guards
faced them with their Stem
guns. After glazing at each
other for several minutes, the
two groups withdrew.

Guinea, Aug. IS (AP).-Rear

mander of Dutch armed forces
fighting Indonesian paratroops

The order is in accordance
with the agreement signed
Thursday at United Nations
headquarters between Holland
and Indonesia to settle their
long dispute over New Guinea


Dutch troops were ordered to

they should try to ascertain
whether their opponents know
about the cease fire.


The Dutch announced what

United Nations.

killed.

The Civil Aeronautics Board

5-16-inch bolt caused the crash
of a Trans World Airlines
plane near Chicago's Midway
airport on September /. 1861,
killing all 70 aboard.


The report said the Lockheed
Constellation crashed about
nine miles west of the airfield
in good weather about five
minutes after takeoff.


The plane was en- route from
Boston and New York to Los
Angeles and San Francisco.
Testimony from about $50 per-
sons interviewed along the
flight path out Of Chicago in
dicated the flight was proceed
ing normally until less than
two miles from the scene of
the accident. No witnesses to
the impact were found.


The plane burst into flames
and was destroyed; the five
crew members and 70 passen-
gers died instantly.


The CAB said its investiga-
ton revealed that a small,
nickel steel bolt was missing
from the elevator boost mech
anism, and was not in place
when the airliner, out Of con-
troll, struck the ground.


THE proper positioning Of
this bolt is vital to the control
Of the aircraft and must there
fore have been in place until
Immediately prior to the loss of
control" the report said.

ruffled in the process were the feelings

westbound traffic thinned out. Some
were delayed as much as IS minutes.

the greater number is best for all had
been supported. Thus, Maryland high

bumper torture. And the State has
been spared, at least for now, the need

Utilities acted a little better

ground remained favorable on

larry higher. Government bonds
were unchanged.

NEW YORK, April 2 (AP).-
The stock market moved ir-
regularly lower in moderate
trading early this afternoon.


Gains and losses of most key
stocks were small. A good
number were unchanged.


Among specially situated or
more volatile stocks there were
some wider losses.


Steels were narrowly mixed
after the agreement on a new
labor contract. General re-
action was luke warm. Big
three motors showed virtually
no change. Rails lost ground
on balance.


Alrlines and farm imple-
mentS took a string of small
losses. Most other groups were
thoroughly scrambled.


Various reports indicated that
the business recovery is slower
than expected; but Wall Street
sentiment was generally opti-
mistic for the spring although
hesitant over the near term.


Prices we're mixed in moder-
